title: Costilla County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Costilla County wells have a 170-foot median depth and 10 gpm median yield. See drilling costs, water levels and checks before buying land.
h1: What to Expect from a Well in Costilla County
intro_html:
A cheap lot in Costilla County is not necessarily a cheap place to get water. Countywide, the median reported well depth is 170 feet, but the middle half runs from 100–280 feet. That spread matters when you price land and construction together.

Colorado DWR records contain 4,161 permitted wells in the county, with 2,565 recorded as constructed. These figures cover the whole county, not just your road or subdivision. Start with the county picture, then check nearby completed wells around Fort Garland, Blanca, San Luis or San Acacio before committing to a parcel.

sections.heading: A 170-Foot Median Is a Starting Point, Not a Bid
sections.html:
Of the 2,615 wells reporting depth, the median is 170 feet and the middle half is 100–280 feet. For a buyer, that means a bid built around the median needs room for additional drilling. The 90th-percentile depth is 400 feet; the deepest reported well reaches 1325 feet.

The cost model describes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. Permit aquifer labels are less specific: 3,818 fall under unnamed / fractured-bedrock aquifer, while other records identify the unconfined San Luis Valley aquifer. That broad unnamed category does not establish the geology beneath a particular lot. Compare nearby completion logs and the water-bearing materials encountered rather than treating the county median as a target depth.

sections.heading: Reported Yields Usually Support a Household Conversation
sections.html:
The 1,108 records with pump yields show a median of 10.0 gpm, with the middle half at 7.0–15.0 gpm. Those results are encouraging for household planning, but a reported pump yield is not a guarantee of sustained production or permission to use water outdoors.

Only 1% of reported yields are under 1 gpm, while 8% fall in the 1–5 gpm band. Low-output wells are therefore a real concern even though they are not typical of the reported sample. Before buying an existing well, request a pumping and recovery test. If output is limited, have the contractor evaluate storage and household demand rather than simply installing a larger pump.

sections.heading: Costilla Water Levels Do Not Show a Clear Declining Trend
sections.html:
Static water level means the depth to water when the well is at rest, not the total drilled depth. Among 532 reporting wells, the median is 80 feet below ground, and the middle half is 45–160 feet. A pump still needs to be selected around pumping conditions, not just that resting level.

Median measured levels were 85 feet in the 1970s, 80 feet in the 2010s and 88 feet in the 2020s. These figures do not establish a steady countywide decline. They also are not repeated measurements from an identical set of wells. For a property decision, recent measurements and recovery behavior at the actual well carry more weight.

sections.heading: Permit Activity and Drillers in the County Record
sections.html:
Costilla County's records include 336 permits issued in the 1970s, 669 in the 1990s and 762 in the 2010s. The 2020s contain 625 permits, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. Permit issuance shows activity, not proof that every authorized well was completed.

The most active drillers listed are Heersink Drilling (Heersink, Scott), with 375 records; Mitchell Drilling Co. (Mitchell Jr., John C.), with 337; and Ojo Spring Drilling & Well Service (Blouin, Octave George), with 230. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. When seeking bids, ask about experience near your parcel and request an explanation of the neighboring completion logs.

sections.heading: Budget Beyond the Drilled Hole in Costilla County
sections.html:
The local model uses $50–$75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 170-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $8,500–$12,800. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $14,500–$24,800.

Treat those amounts as planning figures, not a parcel-specific quote. A deeper completion, difficult access or a longer utility route can change the scope. Ask bidders to spell out casing, grout, testing and what happens if drilling does not produce usable water. The 100–280-foot middle-half depth range is a good reason to request clear per-foot pricing and a written allowance for work beyond the initial estimate.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and Site Constraints Before Closing
sections.html:
The environmental map identifies 6 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 7 historic mine features within about 10 miles. It lists 0 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites in that search area. These are screening results: proximity does not establish contamination in a well, and the absence of a cleanup listing does not establish safe drinking water.

Have a laboratory test the property's water and discuss additional testing with local health officials based on nearby features. Review casing, grout and the wellhead's protection from surface drainage. For vacant land, coordinate the well location with septic approval, the building site and drilling access. Productive neighboring wells help assess risk, but they cannot guarantee a successful hole on your parcel.

sections.heading: Buying Near Blanca or San Luis: Verify the Actual Permit
sections.html:
Before closing on land near Blanca, San Luis, Fort Garland or San Acacio, match the parcel to its DWR permit and available completion records. Verify the permitted uses rather than relying on a listing that says “domestic well.” An exempt household-use permit does not automatically authorize irrigation, livestock watering or every proposed use.

Water availability and legal permission are separate questions. In over-appropriated basins, some proposed uses may require augmentation; confirm the applicable requirements with DWR before designing the project. Then compare nearby depths and yields, obtain a site-specific drilling estimate, and lay out access, septic and utilities together. An existing permit alone is not evidence of a completed, serviceable water supply.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Costilla County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 170 feet, and the middle half of wells runs from 100–280 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 400 feet. Those countywide figures help with budgeting, but nearby completion logs are more useful for a particular parcel because water-bearing materials and required completion depths vary.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Costilla County?
faq.a: The model uses $50–$75 per foot. At the county's 170-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $8,500–$12,800, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $14,500–$24,800. Get a written site-specific quote that explains casing, testing, access requirements and charges for additional depth.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Costilla County?
faq.a: Among 1,108 records reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gpm and the middle half is 7.0–15.0 gpm. Reported yields under 1 gpm account for 1%. Test an existing well's pumping performance and recovery before purchase; a historical yield does not establish its current sustained output.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Costilla County?
faq.a: Safety has to be established by testing the specific well. The mapped area includes 6 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 7 historic mine features within about 10 miles, but those locations do not prove a well is contaminated. Review nearby features, inspect well construction and ask local health officials about appropriate laboratory testing.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Costilla County?
faq.a: The supplied measurements do not show a steady countywide decline. Median static water levels were 85 feet below ground in the 1970s, 80 feet in the 2010s and 88 feet in the 2020s. These are different groups of recorded measurements, not a continuous monitoring history for the well you might buy.
